title: Queues: moving slow work out of the request

claims.text: Little proved the queuing formula in Operations Research in 1961, volume 9, pages 383 to 387: in a queuing process, where one over lambda is the mean time between arrivals of two consecutive units, L is the mean number of units in the system and W is the mean time spent by a unit in the system, then if the three means are finite and the corresponding stochastic processes strictly stationary, and if the arrival process is metrically transitive with nonzero mean, L equals lambda times W.

source.title: John D. C. Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W, Operations Research 9(3):383-387, June 1961, doi 10.1287/opre.9.3.383

claims.text: The relationship is not influenced by the arrival process distribution, the service distribution, the service order, or practically anything else; it applies to any such system, and particularly to systems within systems. Little revisited it fifty years later and reported its use across operations management and computer architecture.

source.title: John D. C. Little, OR FORUM - Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary, Operations Research 59(3):536-549, June 2011, doi 10.1287/opre.1110.0940

beats.broke: a request arrives needing work that takes far longer than the caller is willing to wait, and doing it inline holds a connection, a thread and the caller's attention for the whole duration
beats.fix: accept the request, record the work as a message, answer immediately, and let a separate worker perform it — which decouples the rate at which work arrives from the rate at which it is done
beats.cost: the queue converts a slow response into a pending one, so the caller now needs a way to learn the outcome, and any sustained mismatch between arrival rate and service rate shows up as an unbounded backlog rather than as an error
beats.interview: what a growing queue is actually telling you
